events.c: The bomber group departed Soluch. Lady Be Good's exact takeoff time isn't known.
Lady Be Good took off on April 4. The exact time isn't known.
Sand and poor visibility disrupted the formation. Lady Be Good returned separately from the other bombers.
The group bombed Naples harbor. Lady Be Good's position and altitude during the attack are unknown.
The navigator noted a return course. The exact time isn't known.
The crew released the bombs, but where they fell is unknown.
The crew requested radio directions after their direction finder malfunctioned.
Personnel near Soluch heard a bomber and fired flares. It was probably Lady Be Good.
The pilot's call may have gone unanswered because a radio station suspected an enemy aircraft.
The bomber ran out of fuel. Three propellers were later found set to reduce drag.
The crew parachuted into the desert early on April 5. The exact time isn't known.
The empty bomber struck the desert and skidded about 700 yards. An engine detached and the body broke.
Lady Be Good and another bomber were still missing when the group sent its initial summary.
Eight crew members gathered without the bombardier and walked northwest, sharing food and half a canteen of water.
The crew rested during the day, then walked through the night with frequent short breaks.
The crew reached dunes in blowing sand. They were weakening, and their eyes were affected.
The engineer and two gunners continued to seek help. Five crew members stayed behind.
The engineer's last diary entry describes struggling through dunes for water. His exact time of death is unknown.
The copilot's last diary entry describes another cold night without help. Exact times of death are unknown.
A British convoy reportedly buried unidentified remains in 1953. A connection to the missing gunner remains unproved.
Oil surveyors reportedly spotted the wreck in May and June 1958. The first sighting's date is uncertain.
An aerial sighting was also reported in November 1958. Whether it was the first remains uncertain.
Oil surveyors reached and examined the wreck in early 1959. The exact date is uncertain.
Army and Air Force personnel investigated the empty wreck and began searching for the crew.
Searchers found flight boots north of the wreck, then discarded equipment and arrows made from parachutes.
Another arrow made from parachute material and stones was found. Its exact location is uncertain.
The first search ended without finding remains. Searchers thought sand had covered them.
An investigation report covered the lost bomber and the 1959 search.
Oil workers found five crew members' remains together, along with equipment and the copilot's diary.
Army and Air Force teams searched by ground and air for the four crew members still missing.
Oil workers found a gunner's remains farther north in May 1960.
A helicopter search found the flight engineer's remains and recovered his diary.
The organized search ended in late May 1960. Two crew members were still missing.
A second investigation report covered the final organized search.
The bombardier's remains lay near the descent area with a partially opened parachute. Equipment marked the survivors' gathering.
A memorial window honoring the crew was unveiled at Wheelus, then moved to the U.S. Air Force museum.
A Royal Air Force team recovered components to study how long desert exposure affected the materials.
Libyan authorities moved the remaining wreckage to Tobruk for safekeeping in 1994.
A photograph of the unidentified remains could not establish their identity. The missing gunner's case remained unresolved.

one_line: After overshooting its Libyan base, the crew parachuted into the desert; all nine died.
status_why: The wreck, remains, and diaries explain the loss; precise navigation failures and one crew member's whereabouts remain unresolved.
